q: Which large island lies just south of the Australian mainland, separated from it by Bass Strait?
explain: Tasmania is Australia's island state, a wild and green place famous for its national parks and Tasmanian devils.

q: Which ocean washes along Australia's west coast?
explain: The Indian Ocean lies to Australia's west, while the Pacific Ocean lies to the east.

q: Which famous steel arch bridge, nicknamed 'The Coathanger', spans Sydney Harbour?
explain: The Sydney Harbour Bridge opened in 1932, and its big arch looks like a coat hanger — hence the nickname.

q: Which country lies directly north of Australia, across the narrow Torres Strait?
explain: Papua New Guinea sits just north of Australia's Cape York Peninsula, across the Torres Strait.

q: New Zealand is made up of two main islands — what are they called?
options: The North Island and the South Island
The North Island and Stewart Island
The East Island and the West Island
The North Island and the Chatham Islands
explain: New Zealand's two main islands are simply called the North Island and the South Island.

q: Which of New Zealand's two main islands is the larger one?
explain: The South Island is bigger, but most New Zealanders live on the North Island.

q: What are the indigenous people of New Zealand called?
explain: The Māori are the indigenous people of New Zealand, with a rich culture of carving, song, and dance.

q: Which fuzzy green fruit, originally called the Chinese gooseberry, is New Zealand famous for growing?
explain: Kiwifruit grow mainly in the Bay of Plenty, and New Zealand ships them all over the world.

q: Which Australian city is famous for its laneways, coffee culture, street art, and hosting the Australian Open tennis?
explain: Melbourne, on the Yarra River, is Australia's sporting and cultural capital.

q: What is the highest mountain in Australia?
explain: Mount Kosciuszko, in the Snowy Mountains of New South Wales, stands at 2,228 metres.

q: The Great Barrier Reef lies off the coast of which Australian state?
explain: The reef stretches along Queensland's northeast coast, near towns like Cairns and Port Douglas.

q: Which Australian rock band, formed in Sydney in 1973, is famous for songs like 'Highway to Hell' and 'Back in Black'?
explain: AC/DC, with Angus Young's school-uniform look and roaring guitar riffs, became one of the world's biggest rock bands.

q: Which is the largest desert in Australia?
explain: The Great Victoria Desert stretches across parts of South Australia and Western Australia.

q: Which strait separates New Zealand's North Island from its South Island?
explain: Cook Strait, named after Captain James Cook, is a wild, windy stretch of water between the two main islands.

q: Which huge volcanic lake in the North Island is the largest lake in New Zealand?
explain: Lake Taupō fills the crater of an ancient volcano and is a favourite spot for swimming and boating.

q: Which South Island city, nicknamed the 'Garden City', is famous for its botanic gardens and punting on the Avon River?
explain: Christchurch, on the east coast of the South Island, is known as the Garden City for its beautiful parks and gardens.

q: Which New Zealand film director brought 'The Lord of the Rings' trilogy to life, filming it in his home country?
explain: Peter Jackson, from Wellington, directed The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit films in New Zealand's stunning landscapes.

q: The Murray River forms much of the border between which two Australian states?
options: New South Wales and South Australia
explain: The Murray winds along the New South Wales–Victoria border before reaching the sea in South Australia.

q: What is the name of the vast, treeless limestone plain across southern Australia, whose name is Latin for 'no trees'?
explain: The Nullarbor, from the Latin nullus arbor ('no tree'), is famous for its long, straight roads and underground caves.

q: Which sea lies between northern Australia and the island of New Guinea?
explain: The Arafura Sea fills the shallow shelf between Australia's north coast and New Guinea.

q: Which Australian desert is famous for its long, parallel red sand dunes?
explain: The Simpson Desert, in central Australia, is criss-crossed by hundreds of parallel red dunes.

q: Which nocturnal, flightless parrot, found only in New Zealand, is one of the world's rarest birds?
explain: The kākāpō is a chubby, green, night-time parrot that cannot fly — conservationists work hard to save it.

q: What is the name of the Māori meeting ground, centred on a carved wooden meeting house?
explain: A marae is the heart of Māori community life, with its carved meeting house (wharenui) at the centre.

q: Which group of islands lies about 800 kilometres east of New Zealand in the Pacific Ocean?
explain: The Chatham Islands are part of New Zealand, though they lie far out in the Pacific east of the South Island.

q: New Zealand sits on the boundary of which two tectonic plates?
options: The Nazca and South American plates
explain: The Pacific and Australian plates meet under New Zealand, which is why the country has so many earthquakes and volcanoes.

q: Which spectacular bird, famous for its dazzling plumes, is the national emblem of Papua New Guinea?
explain: Birds of paradise live in the rainforests of New Guinea, and the males dance with their brilliant feathers to impress a mate.

q: Which ocean lies along Papua New Guinea's northern and eastern coasts?
explain: Papua New Guinea's shores open onto the vast Pacific, the biggest ocean on Earth.

q: Which English-based creole language is one of the three official languages of Papua New Guinea?
explain: Tok Pisin grew from the English words used by traders and is now spoken across Papua New Guinea, alongside English and Hiri Motu.

q: Papua New Guinea became an independent country in 1975, after being administered by which nation?
explain: Australia ran Papua New Guinea for decades before the country chose independence in 1975.

q: Which long river in northern Papua New Guinea is famous for the woodcarvings and art of the villages along its banks?
explain: The Sepik winds through northern New Guinea, and its villages are famous for crocodile-shaped masks and carved spirit houses.

q: Which people of the Papua New Guinea Highlands are famous for their spectacular ceremonial wigs woven from their own hair?
explain: Huli wigmen grow their hair for years and shape it into huge golden wigs for colourful sing-sing festivals.

q: Which people of Papua New Guinea's Eastern Highlands are famous for their ghostly white clay mud masks?
explain: The Asaro mudmen wear pale clay masks and costumes to tell stories and perform at festivals in the highlands.

q: About how many islands make up the nation of Fiji?
explain: Fiji has roughly 300 islands, though only about a hundred of them are lived on.

q: What are the names of Fiji's two largest islands?
explain: Viti Levu and Vanua Levu are the two big islands that most visitors to Fiji explore.

q: Which sport is Fiji's national passion, with a world-famous men's sevens team?
explain: Fiji's rugby sevens team is one of the best in the world, and rugby is played everywhere from villages to the Olympics.

q: Which traditional drink, made from the ground root of a pepper plant, is shared in Fijian welcome ceremonies?
explain: Kava, also called yaqona, is a mild, earthy drink sipped from a bowl during Fijian ceremonies and gatherings.

q: Many Fijians are descended from labourers brought from which country to work on sugar cane plantations in the late 1800s and early 1900s?
explain: Thousands of Indian labourers came to Fiji to cut sugar cane, and their descendants now make up a big part of the population.

q: What is the highest mountain in Fiji, on the island of Viti Levu?
explain: Tomanivi, once called Mount Victoria, rises 1,324 metres in the highlands of Viti Levu.

q: Which is the longest river in Fiji, flowing across the island of Viti Levu?
explain: The Rewa is Fiji's longest river and flows into the sea on the south coast of Viti Levu.

q: Which sea, dotted with small islands, lies in the middle of Fiji, ringed by Viti Levu, Vanua Levu and the Lau Islands?
explain: The Koro Sea is enclosed by Fiji's islands: Viti Levu to the west, Vanua Levu to the north and the Lau group to the east.

q: About how many islands make up the archipelago of Vanuatu?
explain: Vanuatu is a chain of roughly 80 islands, and about 65 of them have people living on them.

q: Which island nation lies directly to the east of Vanuatu?
explain: Fiji sits just east of Vanuatu, across the water in the South Pacific.

q: Which sea lies between Australia and Vanuatu?
explain: The Coral Sea stretches between Australia's northeast coast and the islands of Vanuatu and New Caledonia.

q: Which English-based creole language is one of Vanuatu's three official languages?
explain: Bislama mixes English with local languages and is the language most people in Vanuatu speak every day.

q: Which active volcano on the island of Tanna can visitors walk up to and peer down into its glowing crater?
explain: Mount Yasur on Tanna is one of the world's most accessible active volcanoes, rumbling and spitting lava almost every day.

q: What is the highest point in Vanuatu, on the island of Espiritu Santo?
explain: Mount Tabwemasana rises 1,879 metres through the cloud forest of Espiritu Santo, Vanuatu's largest island.

q: Before independence in 1980, Vanuatu was called the New Hebrides and was unusual because it was ruled jointly by which two countries?
explain: The New Hebrides was a rare condominium, where Britain and France shared control until Vanuatu became independent in 1980.

q: The Solomon Islands are named after which biblical king?
explain: A Spanish explorer named the islands in 1568 after King Solomon, hoping they held his legendary gold.

q: About how many islands make up the Solomon Islands?
explain: The Solomon Islands spread across roughly a thousand islands, though only a few hundred are inhabited.

q: Which country lies directly to the west of the Solomon Islands?
explain: Papua New Guinea sits just west of the Solomon Islands, across the water in the Pacific.

q: What is the largest island of the Solomon Islands?
explain: Guadalcanal is the biggest island in the chain, a long, mountainous island in the south.

q: Which musical instrument, made from a row of bamboo pipes, is traditional in the Solomon Islands?
explain: Solomon Islands panpipes, made from bound bamboo tubes, are played at festivals and ceremonies across the islands.

q: What is the highest point of the Solomon Islands, on the island of Guadalcanal?
explain: Mount Popomanaseu rises 2,335 metres above Guadalcanal, deep in the island's rainforest.

q: Which atoll in the Solomon Islands is the world's largest raised coral atoll and a UNESCO World Heritage site?
explain: East Rennell, part of Rennell Island, is a huge raised coral atoll whose lake and forests are protected by UNESCO.
